cards.confidenceNote: Declaration text quoted by BBC and The Guardian (both read); outcome assessments are analysts' views.
cards.title: Trump, Xi and Putin issue joint declaration at first three-way summit
cards.summary: The three leaders met for about 90 minutes in Shenzhen on 19 November and issued a declaration that nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. It called for UN reform, more oil supply and limits on the International Criminal Court, and did not mention Ukraine or Iran.
cards.body:
The Shenzhen meeting was the first three-way session of US, Chinese and Russian leaders, held on the sidelines of APEC after separate Trump-Putin and Trump-Xi bilaterals the same day. Its written output is short. The nuclear sentence repeats the formula the five permanent Security Council members adopted in 2022, so it restates an existing commitment rather than creating a new one. There is no number, no verification step and no date for talks, and Xi used the occasion to repeat China's long-standing call for nuclear weapons to be prohibited over time, the argument Beijing uses to stay out of US-Russia style limits.

What the declaration includes says as much as what it leaves out. Oil supply and UN reform give each leader a deliverable at home; the clause on the International Criminal Court protects officials of all three states. The two wars the participants are fighting or backing, Ukraine and Iran, are absent. Kyiv and European capitals read that absence as a sign that great-power bargaining can proceed over their heads; Britain's opposition leader called the meeting disturbing and Zelensky said big powers cannot decide the world's fate.

The summit is engagement, not a change in posture: its content is declaratory. It does mean the nuclear-risk channel among the three now has a leaders' text to point to; whether officials follow it with talks is the testable next step.

The Russian side paired summitry with pressure: the next morning Russian cruise missiles crashed in Poland during one of the war's largest attacks, and earlier in the week Russian bombers flew to Vietnam. China, meanwhile, began licensing exports of drone engines Russia relies on, a narrow but real constraint that Kyiv welcomed while saying many components remain uncontrolled.

cards.confidenceNote: Plea, alert and listing read on Military Times, Breaking Defense, BBC and Al Jazeera pages; the ship-cyber probe rests on a WSJ report carried by gCaptain.
cards.title: US Army sergeant pleads guilty to passing HIMARS secrets to China
cards.summary: Army supply sergeant Jian Zhao pleaded guilty on 24 November to conspiring to pass defence information, including HIMARS material, to China-connected people. Britain warned defence firms of Russian proxy arson the same day. The US blacklisted Megaspeed on 23 November, and the WSJ reports a probe of suspected Iranian cyberattacks on up to 50 ships.
cards.body:
Four cases in three days show the technology contest running on several fronts at once, and each points at a different adversary.

The Zhao plea is the China file. A supply sergeant at Joint Base Lewis-McChord admitted conspiring from late 2021 to early 2025 to sell national defence information, including excerpts of HIMARS technical manuals, photographs of restricted briefings and government computers, to people connected to China; a co-conspirator had already pleaded guilty and sentencing is set for 1 March 2027. HIMARS is the long-range rocket system at the centre of US plans for Taiwan and the Philippines, so the target matters more than the sums involved, which were small.

The Megaspeed listing is the export-control file. On 23 November the Commerce Department added the Singapore data-centre firm at the centre of the Nvidia diversion affair, and six other Southeast Asian firms, to its Entity List; Singapore opened its own investigation. Beijing has not yet answered, and the board will watch whether it uses its own licensing tools on rare earths or drone parts in reply, as it did in October.

The Russia file is sabotage rather than theft. Britain's protective security agency, run by MI5, told defence firms and suppliers to Ukraine on 24 November that Russia has stepped up attempts to sabotage European defence sites, mainly through arson by low-level proxies hired online. It is a warning, not a new incident, but it formalises what Estonia, Germany and Denmark have attributed case by case, and it comes a week after the US charged a Russian with spying on Palantir staff in California.

The Iran file is the least certain. The Wall Street Journal reported on 23 November that US authorities are investigating suspected cyberattacks on as many as 50 tankers and chemical carriers, some sent bomb threats, with Iran the main suspect and Russia a possible one. No US agency has attributed the attacks on the record, and Reuters could not verify the report. If it holds, the Hormuz confrontation has a cyber front against commercial shipping alongside the drones and projectiles UKMTO logs.

What would change the picture: a named US attribution of the ship attacks; a Chinese counter-listing after Megaspeed; or a first sabotage incident in Britain tied to the proxies the alert describes.

cards.confidenceNote: UKMTO and JMIC counts via gCaptain (read); US alert via Euronews; Iranian mine claims are statements of record only; no attribution of any strike.
cards.title: Hormuz shipping attacks reach ten tankers as Iran blacklists tugboats
cards.summary: gCaptain counts 10 tankers reported struck near Hormuz between 16 and 22 November, none attributed. Iran blacklisted 26 tugboats on 24 November and claims tankers hit mines on 25 November. The IMO counts 25 seafarers dead. The US told citizens to leave Iran on 25 November.
cards.body:
The fighting around Hormuz has moved off Iranian territory and onto the shipping lane. Since the US strike on Qeshm on 17 November, the board has no confirmed US strike on Iran, yet the attack count on merchant ships has risen fastest of any measure: UKMTO reported three tankers struck while sailing east through the strait on 22 November and a bulk carrier set on fire off Khor Fakkan, and gCaptain's tally of reported tanker strikes since 16 November reached ten. None has been attributed by UKMTO or CENTCOM.

Iran's own moves widen the pressure without a named shooter. Its Persian Gulf Strait Authority added 26 tugboats to the blacklist of 'non-compliant' traffic on 24 November, the first time it has listed service craft rather than ships. Its Guard said two tankers hit mines on 25 November, and its army claimed a tanker hit a mine in a 'restricted zone' the same day; neither named a ship, and AP could not confirm. The claims fit a pattern in which Iran asserts control of the strait's rules while declining responsibility for specific hits.

The toll is cumulative and institutional. The IMO counts 141 incidents and 25 seafarers confirmed dead across the crisis as of 23 November, and insurer The Swedish Club told members to avoid the strait unless passage is essential. Traffic has not stopped: independent monitoring cited by the club counted about 26.5 facilitated transits a day on 15-18 November, which is why the board keeps the strait's status at contested rather than closed.

The US signal on 25 November cuts the other way from the lull on land. The embassy alert told Americans to leave Iran immediately because hostilities could escalate rapidly, and Trump said the war is funded through the end of January. Neither is a strike, and the methodology treats preparation as preparation. The tactical question for the next week is whether the US answers the shipping campaign at sea, by seizing or striking a blockade runner, or on Iranian soil, and whether anyone attributes the November strikes.

cards.confidenceNote: US alert via Euronews; Trump remarks via Times of Israel; Iran position via Iran International and The New Arab (analysis); Iran reopening terms on board from 23 Nov.
cards.title: Talks with Iran stall as US tells citizens to leave
cards.summary: Indirect US-Iran contacts are deadlocked, with Iran holding to its conditions for reopening Hormuz. Iran offered on 23 November to reopen the strait within two days if hostilities, the blockade and sanctions end. On 25 November the US told its citizens to leave Iran, and Trump said the war is funded through January.
cards.body:
The diplomatic track has narrowed to two incompatible offers. Iran's foreign ministry said on 23 November that it could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if hostilities, the blockade and sanctions end, while vowing 'all available means' against the blockade. Washington's position, as Trump set it out to Fox News, is that the preliminary Islamabad understanding was 'a waste of time' and that he will finish the war 'one way or the other'. On 12 November he told the Vice-President to drop the talks.

Contacts have not ended. Kushner says meetings with Tehran officials continue under Vance's oversight and that all options remain on the table, but reporting from the region describes the indirect channel as deadlocked, with Iran not moving on its conditions. Qatar, the main mediator, is under strain: Iran summoned its envoy on 23 November over a joint Qatar-Germany statement, and a Qatari delegation's 20 November visit to Tehran produced no announced result.

Two US statements on 25 November shift the frame from talks to timing. The embassy alert told Americans to leave Iran immediately, warning that hostilities could escalate rapidly and that Iran, the Houthis and aligned groups may target US interests. Trump said the war is funded through the end of January, which sets a horizon without setting a date. Iran's Guard answered with warnings of 'new targets, weapons and offensive plans' if the US or Israel 'make another mistake'.

The board reads this as a stalled track with escalation risk rising, not a broken one: mediators remain engaged and no party has declared talks over. The deal that matters, reopening the strait in exchange for lifting the blockade, has the same shape it had in June; what has changed is that each side now conditions it on the other moving first. An agreement before 30 November looks very unlikely.

cards.confidenceNote: Gaza strikes via France 24 and BBC (on board); Netanyahu trial development read at BBC; joint strike planning is one NYT report.
cards.title: Judges urge dropping Netanyahu charges as Israel hits Hamas leaders
cards.summary: Judges in Netanyahu's corruption trial suggested on 25 November that prosecutors drop the bribery charges. An Israeli strike killed Hamas's internal security chief in Gaza on 24 November. Eisenkot, who holds the mandate to form a government, faces a 6 December deadline.
cards.body:
Israel's war in Gaza has become a campaign against Hamas's security leadership under a ceasefire that both sides say the other violates. An Israeli strike killed the head of Hamas's internal security apparatus on 24 November. It follows the 18 November armoured incursion across the ceasefire line, which displaced 5,200 people, and the killing of the Rafah brigade commander on 14 November.

On Iran, the New York Times reported that US and Israeli officials have drawn up plans for renewed strikes on energy targets, and on 25 November Trump said the war is funded through the end of January, a horizon that would bound any renewed joint campaign.

Israel's own politics are in flux. Judges in Netanyahu's corruption trial suggested on 25 November that prosecutors drop the bribery charges, a boost for the caretaker prime minister, who called for the trial to end immediately. Eisenkot, who holds the mandate to form a government, faces a 6 December deadline after the Likud-Yashar unity talks collapsed on 22 November.

For the alliance, the question is whether a change of Israeli government changes the Iran calculus. A new coalition would keep the Gaza security campaign but could weigh a second round against Iran differently from Netanyahu, which would leave Washington, not Jerusalem, setting the timetable the funding remark implies.

cards.confidenceNote: Facts read on BBC, Guardian, Al Jazeera pages; scenario weights are the board's judgement.
cards.title: Russian missiles hit Poland a day after the Shenzhen nuclear declaration
cards.summary: Trump, Xi and Putin declared on 19 November that nuclear war must never be fought. On 20 November Russian cruise missiles crashed in Poland during a mass attack on Ukraine, and on 21 November Iran struck Bahrain and tankers near Hormuz. The board's score holds at 66.
cards.body:
The window shows the distance between leaders' declarations and the two wars. The Shenzhen text was the most significant joint statement by the three nuclear powers this year, yet it ignored Ukraine and Iran, and within a day each war produced a fresh escalation step outside its main theatre: Russian missiles inside NATO territory, Iranian fire causing damage at a civilian site in Bahrain.

Both steps sit inside the bands the board already scores. Poland reported no injuries; NATO scrambled jets but did not engage; Warsaw is asking for more air defence rather than invoking collective defence. In the Gulf, the Bahrain attack caused damage but no injuries, and no US retaliation on Iranian soil was confirmed. The four axes therefore hold: kinetic 75, great-power 70, WMD 60, alliance 60.

The European pattern is the week's most consistent signal. Poland calls the missiles intentional, Denmark attributes an assassination plot to Russian intelligence and expelled an attaché, Estonia closes its road border, and Finland says the war is spilling over after a strike on a Russian ship in the Gulf of Finland. These are national responses, coordinated in solidarity statements, not an alliance rupture. At the same time Denmark ratified its Greenland deal with Washington, which removes a source of NATO friction.

What would move the score: a NATO shootdown or a casualty on allied territory; a US strike campaign on Iranian energy targets; deaths in a Gulf state from Iranian fire; or follow-up nuclear talks among the three powers, which would argue the other way.

cards.title: Leaked Rosstat records show at least 490,000 Russian war dead
cards.summary: Meduza and Mediazona found at least 490,000 Russian military deaths registered by late September in leaked Rosstat data; adding the missing, they estimate more than 700,000. The Kremlin declined comment. Poland will create a no-fly zone on its Ukraine border, and both sides struck energy and cities again.
cards.body:
The war's cost to Russia now has a number taken from Russia's own registry. Hackers from the Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow announced a breach of Rosstat on 1 November and gave the records to journalists from 8 November; Meduza and Mediazona cleaned 11.7 million records covering January 2021 to 29 September 2026 and identified at least 490,000 deaths of Russian servicemen already registered. That figure is a floor. Deaths are registered with delays of months, and missing soldiers often a year or more later; modelling those, the authors estimate the true toll at about 700,000 by September, rising to 720,000 or more by the autumn. Other teams working from the leak reached counts of 472,000 to 537,000, the higher ones including foreign nationals. The Kremlin declined to comment, saying only the defence ministry can give figures; it has not done so since September 2022. The board shows the floor and the estimate as two figures, and compares neither with Ukraine's General Staff tally, which counts killed and wounded.

The spillover track is where the war is changing shape. After Russian cruise missiles fell on Polish soil on 20 November and a drone crossed the Lublin region on 23 November, Poland announced a no-fly zone at least 10 km deep along its Ukraine border, with rules due by early January that let pilots engage without visual identification. Trump and Rutte jointly urged Russia to avoid actions that widen the war. Estonia expelled a Russian worker at a border oil plant over intelligence ties, days before its road crossings close on 1 December, and two Libyan soldiers have died of wounds from the Ukrainian-claimed strike on Russian ships at Benghazi.

On the front, both sides are hitting energy. Ukraine reported damaging five jets at Savasleyka and drones reached refineries in Samara and a pumping station in Bashkortostan; Russia struck Kharkiv with ballistic missiles and 113 drones and hit a Kyiv shopping centre. Diplomacy is thin: Kushner says Putin is not interested in a ceasefire, the Abu Dhabi prisoner exchange has not happened, and 48 allied-funded Patriots still await Pentagon sign-off.

iran_lead.title: US tells citizens to leave Iran; Trump says war funded to January
iran_lead.summary: The US told its citizens on 25 November to leave Iran immediately, warning that hostilities could escalate rapidly. Trump said the war is funded through the end of January. Iran's Revolutionary Guard claims two tankers hit mines on 25 November, unconfirmed. No US strike on Iranian territory has been reported since 17 November.
facts: 25 Nov: US tells citizens to leave Iran immediately.
25 Nov: Trump says the Iran war is funded through January.
25 Nov: Houthis claim strikes on Jeddah and Jazan ports and Ras Tanura.
26 Nov: coalition intercepts two missiles fired at Riyadh.
iran_lead.changed: Washington's posture shifted from blockade maintenance toward preparation language: a leave-now alert naming Iran, the Houthis and aligned groups as threats, and a presidential funding horizon that sets a window rather than a date. At sea, the only new claim in the window is Iranian (mine strikes, no ship named). The Houthis widened their Saudi campaign to Red Sea ports and Ras Tanura, and Sky News reports Britain is sheltering RAF aircraft over drone threats and suspected Iran-linked plots.
iran_lead.watch: Any US strike on Iranian territory or on a blockade runner; attribution of the 22 November tanker strikes; whether other governments issue leave-now alerts; Houthi fire on Riyadh; OPEC+ on 29 November.

brics_lead.title: US proposes tariffs up to 20% on China, EU and 12 others
brics_lead.summary: The US Trade Representative proposed tariffs of up to 20% on 14 economies, including China, the EU, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan, on 25 November after a probe into excess capacity. China said it reserves the right to respond; Japan and the EU pushed back. Kim Jong Un called for wider tactical nuclear deployment.
brics_lead.changed: A week after the Shenzhen summit, Washington opened a trade front against its rival and its allies at once: the proposal puts China at 20%, the rate its truce set, with officials signalling 40% if talks fail, and treats Japan, South Korea and the EU as overcapacity producers too. Rates go to public comment before any action in January. In the CRINK lens, Kim called for tactical nuclear weapons spread across more domains.
brics_lead.watch: Beijing's formal countermeasures and whether the truce holds; allied responses in the comment period; Taiwan's 28 November local elections and Chinese pressure around them; further North Korean nuclear moves.

lenses.oneline: The US proposed a 20% tariff on China a week after Shenzhen; Beijing reserves the right to respond.

26 Nov: China's commerce ministry reserves the right to respond.
26 Nov: Kim calls for wider tactical nuclear deployment (state media).
26 Nov: Japan and China trade protests over the Senkakus.

ukraine_lead.title: Leaked Rosstat data puts Russian war dead at 490,000 or more
ukraine_lead.summary: Leaked Rosstat records show at least 490,000 Russian soldiers dead by late September, Meduza and Mediazona found; counting the missing, they estimate more than 700,000. Poland will create a no-fly zone on its Ukraine border. Ukraine says it damaged five jets at Savasleyka; Russian missiles hit Kharkiv and Kyiv.

25 Nov: Poland announces a no-fly zone along the Ukraine border.
25 Nov: Trump and Rutte urge Russia not to widen the war.
25 Nov: Ukraine's General Staff says five jets damaged at Savasleyka.
25 Nov: US consortium signs Lukoil foreign-assets deal, pending OFAC.

On the ground both sides hit energy and cities again.
